set1.q: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, a marrow with about 2% blasts fits which phase?
opts: Blast phase behaves as an acute leukemia, usually like acute myeloid leukemia, with blasts at acute leukemia levels. Tell: 2% blasts is the stable phase.
Acute myeloid leukemia needs myeloid blasts at or above 20% historically. Tell: 2% blasts with a fusion gene is chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia.
Correct. The chronic (stable) phase is the early proliferative phase with no or few blasts, below 5%; 2% blasts fits it. It has an excellent prognosis and accounts for 85-90% of all presentations.
The accelerated phase often has 10-19% blasts, with dysplastic granulocytes, fibrosis and significant splenomegaly. Tell: 2% is well below that band.

set1.q: About what is the overall five-year survival of acute myeloid leukemia?
opts: Five percent is the five-year survival of patients over 70, the lowest group. Tell: the overall figure is about 25-30%.

Correct. Treatment brings initial remission in many patients, but acute myeloid leukemia frequently relapses and treatment-related mortality is high: overall survival is only 48% at one year and about 25-30% at five years.
Forty-eight percent is the overall survival at one year, not at five years. Tell: by five years it falls to about 25-30%.
A cure rate above 90% belongs to acute promyelocytic leukemia in patients who survive the initial presentation. Tell: acute myeloid leukemia overall is about 25-30% at five years.

set1.q: What is the median age at diagnosis of myelodysplastic syndrome?
opts: Under 15 is where acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common malignancy. Tell: myelodysplasia is a disease of older adults.
Around 50 is the adult peak of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and 45 to 55 the median of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: myelodysplasia is older, with a median of 70.
Over 60 is where acute myeloid leukemia is mostly seen. Tell: the median age for myelodysplastic syndrome is higher, 70.
Correct. Myelodysplastic syndrome is often idiopathic and occurs in an older population, with a median age of 70 years. It is more common in men and sometimes follows prior chemotherapy or radiation.

set1.q: Before tyrosine kinase inhibitors, chronic myelogenous leukemia historically progressed to acute leukemia in about how many years?
opts: One to two years understates the historical course of about 4-6 years. Tell: under 2 years is closer to high-risk myelofibrosis survival.

Correct. Chronic myelogenous leukemia historically progressed from a chronic condition to acute leukemia in about 4-6 years and was considered fatal; with tyrosine kinase inhibitors it is now largely a chronic disorder with long-term survival.
Ten to fifteen years is how long low-risk myelofibrosis patients can live. Tell: untreated chronic myelogenous leukemia historically turned acute in about 4-6 years.
Fourteen years is the estimated survival of polycythemia vera. Tell: the historical chronic myelogenous leukemia figure is about 4-6 years to acute leukemia.

set1.q: For an older patient with acute myeloid leukemia who is unfit for intensive chemotherapy, which treatment is used?
opts: Phlebotomy and hydroxyurea are the listed treatment for polycythemia vera. Tell: they are not the low-intensity regimen for unfit acute myeloid leukemia.
Correct. Unfit patients receive low-intensity therapy, frequently a hypomethylating agent with or without venetoclax. Fitness matters most in older patients, and survival is lowest over age 70.
Cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3) is intensive chemotherapy for fit patients. Tell: an unfit patient gets low-intensity therapy instead.
Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid is the unique treatment approach for acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: the unfit acute myeloid leukemia patient gets a hypomethylating agent.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set1.q: Which presentation is typical of myelofibrosis?
opts: Pruritus with warm baths or showers is the classic symptom of polycythemia vera. Tell: abdominal fullness from a big spleen points to myelofibrosis.
A mediastinal mass on chest X-ray may be seen in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: myelofibrosis enlarges the spleen, not the mediastinum.
Gum involvement is a feature of the myelomonocytic and monocytic subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: myelofibrosis symptoms come from splenomegaly.

Correct. Myelofibrosis presents non-specifically with fatigue and abdominal symptoms from splenomegaly, including pain, early satiety and bloating; night sweats, fever and weight loss are also common.

set1.q: What does an allogeneic stem cell transplant use?
opts: Using the person's own stem cells is an autologous transplant, also called stem cell rescue, often given to rescue the marrow after high-dose chemotherapy. Tell: auto means self; allo means a donor.

Red cells and platelets are mature blood cells; they do not replace the marrow the way a stem cell transplant does. Tell: a transplant gives healthy stem cells to a depleted or dysfunctional marrow, not mature blood cells.
Growth factors push the existing marrow; they do not supply new stem cells, so they are not a transplant. Tell: a transplant gives healthy stem cells to a depleted or dysfunctional marrow.
Correct. An allogeneic stem cell transplant uses a healthy donor's stem cells in transplantation, unlike an autologous transplant, which uses the person's own stem cells.

set1.q: In a hematologic malignancy, bleeding is usually due to which count abnormality?
opts: Correct. Hematologic malignancies often present with non-specific symptoms: fatigue from anemia, bleeding from thrombocytopenia, swollen nodes in lymphoma and bone pain in myeloma. Low platelets explain the bruising and bleeding.
Anemia explains fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, shortness of breath and pale skin, not bleeding. Tell: tiredness points to red cells; bleeding points to platelets.
Too few working white cells explains infections, not bleeding. Tell: infections follow ineffective or low white cells, while bruising and bleeding follow low platelets.

A high white count reflects proliferation of the leukemic clone itself; it does not cause bleeding by the stated mechanism. Tell: bleeding is listed under thrombocytopenia, with petechiae and purpura.

set1.q: Acute myeloid leukemia has historically been defined by myeloid blasts at or above what percentage?
opts: Below 5% blasts describes the chronic phase of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: acute leukemia sits at 20% or more.
Ten percent or higher is the newer exception for certain genetic mutations, not the historical definition. Tell: the classic line is 20%.

Correct. Acute myeloid leukemia has historically been defined by myeloid blasts at or above 20%; newer guidelines note that certain genetic mutations may allow the diagnosis with 10% or higher. Below 20%, a dysplastic marrow with blasts is myelodysplastic syndrome.
Thirty percent overstates the definition; the threshold is 20%. Tell: higher-risk myelodysplastic syndrome may have blasts but below 20%, otherwise it is acute myeloid leukemia.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slides 38, 47

set1.q: Which cell characterizes Hodgkin lymphoma?
opts: Plasma cells are the cell of origin of multiple myeloma, which makes a monoclonal M protein. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma is marked by a few Reed-Sternberg cells in a crowd of immune cells.
Arrested promyelocytes define acute promyelocytic leukemia, a myeloid cancer caused by the chromosome 15 and 17 translocation. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma is lymphoid tissue with Reed-Sternberg cells.

Lymphoblasts are the very immature cells of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, which floods the marrow and blood. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma has few malignant cells, the Reed-Sternberg cells, not a flood of blasts.

Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma, about 10% of lymphomas, is characterized by few malignant Reed-Sternberg cells among numerous immune effector cells. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma makes up the other 90% and includes B-cell and T-cell types.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 15

set1.topic: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: who and why
set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for disorders of hematological malignancies in the lecture topic list for the following populations. Infant a. child b. adolescent c. adult d. elderly
set1.q: Which age groups carry the highest risk of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
opts: A median age of 70 belongs to myelodysplastic syndrome, which is often idiopathic in older people. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is bimodal, with a pediatric peak.
A median age of 45 to 55 years describes chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is bimodal, peaking in young children and again after 50.

Correct. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia has a bimodal distribution: risk is highest in children under 5 and adults over 50. It is the most common malignancy under age 15, and in adults incidence peaks around 50.
Adults over 60 are the group at risk for acute myeloid leukemia, which is unusual in children outside neonates. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia has two peaks, one of them in young children.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slides 18, 21

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set1.q: At 6 months of treatment for chronic myelogenous leukemia, the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level is 4%. Which milestone category is this?
opts: At 6 months, failure needs a level above 10%, and 4% is below it. Failure means the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level is above the worst cutoff for that month: above 10% at 6 months, above 1% at 12 months and beyond; it is not defined at 3 months.

Correct. At 6 months, the milestone table reads failure above 10%, warning 1-10% and optimal below 1%. A level of 4% sits between 1% and 10%, so it is a warning; treatment-free remission is not applicable at 6 months.
At 6 months, optimal needs a level below 1%, and 4% is above it. Optimal is below 10% at 3 months, below 1% at 6 months, and below 0.1% at 12 months and beyond.

Treatment-free remission is not applicable at 6 months. Treatment-free remission is defined only beyond 18 months, at a BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level below 0.01%; at earlier months the column is not applicable.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 64

set1.q: What determines whether a hematologic malignancy is lymphoid or myeloid?
opts: Correct. Hematologic malignancies are classified into leukemias, lymphomas and plasma cell disorders, and the underlying cell of origin determines whether the type is lymphoid or myeloid, the two progenitor lines of normal hematopoiesis.

Symptoms such as fatigue, bleeding, swollen nodes or bone pain are non-specific and overlap across the families. Tell: the lineage label follows the cell the cancer started from, not how the patient feels.
A white count measures how many cells there are, not which progenitor line the cancer came from. Tell: lineage follows the cell of origin; the count only shows how many cells there are.
Age shifts the likelihood of a given cancer, but it does not define lineage. Tell: lineage is a property of the cancer cell's origin, not of the patient.

set1.topic: Myelodysplastic syndrome
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: What defines myelodysplastic syndromes?
opts: Atypical proliferation of mature cell lines defines the myeloproliferative neoplasms: polycythemia vera, myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia. Tell: myelodysplasia means abnormal-looking cells and low counts.

Marrow fibrosis is not the defining feature; myelodysplastic syndromes are defined by dysplasia of myeloid cells. Tell: myelodysplastic syndrome is defined by dysplasia, with a typically hypercellular marrow.
Myeloid blasts at or above 20% define acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: higher-risk myelodysplastic syndrome may have blasts, but below 20%.

Correct. Myelodysplastic syndromes are a group of myeloid malignancies defined by dysplasia (abnormal appearance) of myeloid cells, with distorted hematopoiesis, immune dysregulation and genomic changes. They present as cytopenias, most often anemia.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slides 45, 47, 51

set1.q: Where does normal hematopoiesis begin?
opts: The spleen is a lymphoid tissue in which some lymphomas arise, but blood cell production does not begin there. Tell: the stem cell that starts hematopoiesis lives in the bone marrow.

The thymus is a lymphoid tissue where some lymphomas and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia can be found, not where hematopoiesis begins. Tell: the hematopoietic stem cell sits in the marrow, upstream of every lymphoid and myeloid line.

Correct. Normal hematopoiesis begins in the bone marrow with hematopoietic stem cells, which differentiate into myeloid and lymphoid progenitors and then into the terminally differentiated cell lines.

Lymph nodes are lymphoid tissue where lymphomas often arise, not the starting point of blood cell production. Tell: hematopoiesis starts with stem cells in the marrow; lymph nodes are where lymphoma cells collect.

set1.q: In chronic myelogenous leukemia, about 14% blasts with significant splenomegaly fits which phase?
opts: Correct. The accelerated phase often has 10-19% blasts, may show dysplastic granulocytes and fibrosis, and frequently presents with significant splenomegaly; 14% blasts sits inside that band. It is about 4-5% of presentations.
The chronic (stable) phase has no or few blasts, below 5%, and makes up 85-90% of presentations. Tell: 14% blasts is far above the chronic-phase level.
Blast phase, or blast crisis, behaves as an acute leukemia, usually like acute myeloid leukemia, which is defined by 20% or more blasts. Tell: 14% is below the acute leukemia line.

Myelodysplastic syndrome also has blasts below 20%, but it presents as cytopenias, not with the marked leukocytosis and fusion gene of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: the stem names a chronic myelogenous leukemia phase question.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slides 38, 47, 62

set1.q: What sorts acute myeloid leukemia into favorable, intermediate and poor risk?
opts: The blast percentage, 20% or more, makes the diagnosis rather than the risk group. Tell: once diagnosed, cytogenetics and mutations sort the risk.

The performance grade measures fitness and steers intensive versus low-intensity therapy, but it is not the basis of the genetic risk groups. Tell: favorable, intermediate and poor risk are read from cytogenetics and mutations.

Correct. Acute myeloid leukemia shows tremendous variety in cytogenetic abnormalities and mutations, and risk is broken down into favorable, intermediate and poor on that basis. Cytogenetic and mutation analysis is important for prognosis.
The white count is often elevated but may be low, and counts above 100,000 need leukapheresis; it does not set the risk group. Tell: the risk categories come from the genetics.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set1.q: Which treatment is unique to acute promyelocytic leukemia?
opts: Correct. Acute promyelocytic leukemia has a unique treatment approach: arsenic trioxide and all-trans retinoic acid, rather than the chemotherapy used for other acute myeloid leukemia. Patients who survive the presentation have a cure rate above 90%.

Cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3) is intensive chemotherapy for fit patients with other acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the promyelocytic subtype gets arsenic trioxide and all-trans retinoic acid instead.
Hypomethylating agents, with or without venetoclax, are low-intensity therapy for unfit patients with acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the promyelocytic subtype has its own regimen.

Tyrosine kinase inhibitors treat chronic myelogenous leukemia and Philadelphia-positive lymphoblastic leukemia, the chromosome 9 and 22 diseases. Tell: chromosome 15 and 17 disease gets arsenic and retinoic acid.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set1.q: Why can essential thrombocythemia cause bleeding despite a high platelet count?
opts: Correct. Bleeding with high platelets can occur in essential thrombocythemia because of acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency, leaving a shortage of factor at the site of injury.
Platelets are high, not low, in essential thrombocythemia; thrombocytopenia is the bleeding cause in leukemia. Tell: the paradox is bleeding with high platelets.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the emergent bleeding of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: essential thrombocythemia bleeds from a von Willebrand factor shortage.
Portal hypertension with bleeding is a complication of myelofibrosis. Tell: in essential thrombocythemia the bleeding comes from acquired von Willebrand factor loss.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 54

set1.q: Where is acute lymphoblastic leukemia typically found, in contrast to an aggressive lymphoma?
opts: Bone pain with a monoclonal M protein is multiple myeloma, a malignancy of plasma cells. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is immature lymphoid blasts spread through the marrow and blood.

Correct. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia often shows diffuse marrow and peripheral blood involvement, in contrast to aggressive lymphomas, which involve nodal or extranodal sites with minimal bone marrow involvement.
Nodal or extranodal disease with minimal marrow involvement describes aggressive lymphomas, the reverse of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: the leukemia fills the marrow and blood.
Severe splenomegaly with fibrosis of the marrow is myelofibrosis, the most aggressive of the myeloproliferative neoplasms. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a diffuse marrow and blood disease.

set1.topic: Polycythemia vera
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set1.q: Which mutation commonly causes polycythemia vera?
opts: The BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) fusion from the chromosome 9 and 22 translocation is the hallmark of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: a red cell overproduction disorder points to the Janus kinase 2 mutation.
The PML-RARA (promyelocytic leukemia-retinoic acid receptor alpha) fusion from chromosomes 15 and 17 causes acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera is a Janus kinase 2 disease.
Hyperdiploidy, excess chromosome copies, is the favorable childhood finding in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: the myeloproliferative neoplasms share Janus kinase pathway mutations.
Correct. Polycythemia vera commonly occurs as a result of a JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) mutation. Myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia also arise from mutations in the same Janus kinase pathway.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slide 52

set1.q: Which acute myeloid leukemia subtypes may show gum hyperplasia or other extramedullary disease?
opts: Acute erythroid and acute megakaryocytic leukemias are very rare subtypes, not the ones linked to gum involvement. Tell: extramedullary disease is a monocytic-line feature.
Undifferentiated acute myeloid leukemia is not among the subtypes tied to gum involvement or extramedullary disease. Tell: gum hyperplasia means myelomonocytic or monocytic.
Correct. The myelomonocytic and monocytic subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia tend to have more extramedullary involvement, and they may involve the gums (hyperplasia).
Acute promyelocytic leukemia is a separate subtype, not one of those tied to gum involvement or extramedullary disease. Tell: gums point to the monocytic subtypes.
set1.cite: 49. Hematologic Malignancies Part I - Gannon.pptx, Slides 33, 35

set1.q: How is blast-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia treated?
opts: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor by itself
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark of chronic-phase therapy, but blast phase responds poorly to them. Tell: blast crisis is treated like an acute leukemia.
Watching would ignore a stage that behaves as an acute leukemia with median survival under 12 months. Tell: blast phase needs acute myeloid leukemia-like treatment.
Stopping tyrosine kinase inhibitors is considered only after a sustained major molecular response in chronic-phase disease. Tell: blast phase needs intensive acute leukemia-like treatment.

Correct. Blast phase, or blast crisis, behaves as an acute leukemia, usually like acute myeloid leukemia, often with unique chromosomal and mutational changes; it requires acute myeloid leukemia-like regimens and responds poorly to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

set1.q: What is the classic symptom of polycythemia vera?
opts: Gum involvement (hyperplasia) is seen in the myelomonocytic and monocytic subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the polycythemia vera clue is itch with warm water.
Bone or joint pain from excessive marrow production of leukemia cells is a feature of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera classically itches after warm baths or showers.
Correct. Polycythemia vera usually presents non-specifically with fatigue, headaches and blurry vision, but the classic symptom is pruritus with warm baths or showers.
Early satiety, bloating and abdominal pain from splenomegaly are the presentation of myelofibrosis. Tell: itching after a warm bath is the polycythemia vera clue.

set1.topic: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: who and why
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set1.q: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia originates in which cells?
opts: Correct. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia originates in the lymphoid progenitor or stem cells, very immature cells with a rapid ability to proliferate. Mutagenesis happens at the lymphoblast stage as cells differentiate toward B or T lymphocytes.
Myeloid progenitor cells give rise to acute myeloid leukemia, whose blasts may show Auer rods. Tell: lymphoblastic names the lymphoid line; myeloid leukemia is the other acute leukemia.

set1.q: Why do patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia have bone or joint pain?
opts: Fibrosis is not the cause; the bone or joint pain comes from very excessive marrow production of leukemia cells. Tell: the pain in lymphoblastic leukemia comes from a marrow packed with blasts.

High platelets do not fit; acute lymphoblastic leukemia causes thrombocytopenia, with bruising and bleeding rather than clots. Tell: acute lymphoblastic leukemia lowers platelets; its bone pain is marrow overgrowth.

Correct. B-symptoms are weight loss, fever and night sweats, with loss of appetite listed too. They appear in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia and chronic myelogenous leukemia, and lymphomas often present with night sweats, weight loss and fevers.

Counts above 100,000 are the threshold for emergent leukapheresis in acute myeloid leukemia, not the usual lymphoblastic figure. Tell: the usual lymphoblastic leukemia figure is above 30,000.

Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark of chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia and are used for Philadelphia-positive lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: fit acute myeloid leukemia gets cytarabine plus an anthracycline.

Correct. Fit patients receive intensive chemotherapy, often cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3). Allogeneic stem cell transplant typically follows for most intermediate- and high-risk patients who achieve remission.
Hypomethylating agents, with or without venetoclax, are low-intensity therapy for unfit patients. Tell: fitness decides it, and a fit patient gets intensive chemotherapy.

Correct. The only curative therapy for myelodysplastic syndrome is allogeneic stem cell transplant, using a healthy donor's stem cells, but it is high risk and has a limited role in therapy.
Hypomethylating agents, like chemotherapy, treat higher-risk disease but are not described as curative. Tell: cure requires replacing the marrow with a donor's stem cells.
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents support low-risk anemia and improve quality of life; they do not cure. Tell: the curative option is an allogeneic transplant.

Low counts with abnormal-looking neutrophils describe myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia raises the white count and platelets.

Favorable-risk acute myeloid leukemia has the highest survival outside the promyelocytic subtype, about two thirds alive at five years. Tell: the worst outlook is age over 70.

set2.q: When myeloid growth factors are given for neutropenia in myelodysplastic syndrome, what is the caution?

Coagulopathy is not the stated caution; myeloid growth factors are given for neutropenia with care not to overstimulate blasts. Tell: the growth factor caution in myelodysplasia is blast stimulation.
Marrow fibrosis is not the stated caution; the concern with myeloid growth factors is overstimulation of blasts. Tell: the warning is about stimulating blasts.

The myeloblast level corresponds to the least mature subtypes, undifferentiated and minimal-maturation acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: the name promyelocytic gives the stage away.
Monoblasts are the cells of acute monocytic leukemia, which may involve the gums. Tell: acute promyelocytic leukemia stops at the promyelocyte.

Myeloid versus lymphoid is decided by the underlying cell of origin, a label separate from the acute versus chronic split. Tell: lineage and tempo are separate labels; acute refers to immature cells.
Lymph node involvement is the hallmark of lymphoma, which arises from lymphoid tissue. Tell: a leukemia is a marrow disease; acute versus chronic depends on how immature the cells are.

Presenting mainly in a leukemic phase, with blasts and marrow involvement, describes B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: the T-cell form behaves more like a lymphoma and may involve the thymus.

A fibrotic marrow is not the T-cell feature; T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia usually has lymphoma-like characteristics and may involve the thymus. Tell: T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia is linked with the thymus and a mediastinal mass, not fibrosis.
Correct. T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia is rarer and usually has lymphoma-like characteristics, and it may involve the thymus. A mediastinal mass may be seen on chest X-ray in T-cell disease.

Admission for work-up and treatment is the start for acute leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia are referred to hematology with smoking cessation.
Correct. Patients with polycythemia vera and with essential thrombocythemia should be referred to a hematologist and advised to cease smoking.

Hydroxyurea is shared, but phlebotomy is the polycythemia vera treatment for red cell excess; essential thrombocythemia uses aspirin or hydroxyurea. Tell: the shared advice is referral and smoking cessation.

set2.q: Which viral infection is listed as a risk factor for acute myeloid leukemia?

Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, linked to Caribbean countries, is listed for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: the myeloid list names human immunodeficiency virus instead.
Pertussis is a bacterial infection that can cause an atypical lymphocytosis mimicking acute lymphoblastic leukemia; it is not a risk factor. Tell: it is a mimic, not a cause.

opts: Correct. Essential thrombocythemia is treated with aspirin, hydroxyurea or other agents to reduce clotting risk, and patients are referred to a hematologist and advised to cease smoking.
Phlebotomy lowers the red cell excess of polycythemia vera. Tell: essential thrombocythemia is a platelet problem treated with aspirin or hydroxyurea.
Adding platelets would raise an already high count. Tell: the goal in essential thrombocythemia is to reduce clotting risk, with aspirin or hydroxyurea.

set2.q: Multiple myeloma arises from which cell?
opts: Myeloid progenitors give rise to acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and the myeloproliferative neoplasms. Tell: the name sounds myeloid, but myeloma is a lymphoid-line cancer of antibody-making plasma cells.
Lymphoblasts are the very immature lymphoid cells of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: myeloma comes from the most mature end of the B-cell line, the terminally differentiated plasma cell.

Correct. Multiple myeloma arises from terminally differentiated B cells called plasma cells. Because plasma cells make our antibodies, myeloma produces an excess of a single monoclonal antibody, the M protein.

T cells are lymphoid cells that can give rise to T-cell lymphomas and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, not myeloma. Tell: myeloma is a plasma cell disorder, and plasma cells come from B cells, not T cells.

set2.q: How is Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated?
opts: Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid is the unique treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia, the chromosome 15 and 17 disease. Tell: the 9 and 22 translocation calls for a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
Phlebotomy and hydroxyurea treat polycythemia vera, which overproduces red cells. Tell: a Philadelphia-positive acute leukemia needs a tyrosine kinase inhibitor with chemotherapy.

Hypomethylating agents are low-intensity therapy for unfit patients with acute myeloid leukemia and for higher-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: the Philadelphia chromosome points to a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

Correct. Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia, carrying the chromosome 9 and 22 translocation, is treated with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor plus chemotherapy. Allogeneic transplant is added where feasible for adverse-risk or relapsed disease.

set2.q: How is myelofibrosis often treated?
opts: Arsenic trioxide with all-trans retinoic acid is the unique treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Tell: myelofibrosis treatment is palliative Janus kinase inhibition.
Correct. Myelofibrosis is often treated with targeted inhibitors, Janus kinase inhibitors, which are palliative. Patients should be referred to a hematologist upon diagnosis.
Phlebotomy removes the red cell excess of polycythemia vera. Tell: myelofibrosis gets palliative Janus kinase inhibitors.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the hallmark therapy of chronic-phase chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: myelofibrosis is a Janus kinase pathway disease treated with Janus kinase inhibitors.

set2.q: Which chemical exposure is named as a risk factor for hematologic malignancies?
opts: Aspirin is used to reduce clotting risk in essential thrombocythemia; it is not listed as a risk factor. Tell: the environmental exposures named are radiation and chemicals like benzene.

Correct. Environmental risk factors include radiation and specific chemical exposures such as benzene, alongside genetic factors, autoimmune disorders and older age. Benzene is listed again for both acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemia.

Arsenic trioxide appears as a treatment, used with all-trans retinoic acid for acute promyelocytic leukemia, not as a named risk factor. Tell: the chemical risk factor is benzene; arsenic is on the therapy side.

Hydroxyurea is a treatment for polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia, not a listed cause. Tell: the drugs named as risks are certain chemotherapies such as alkylators; the chemical is benzene.

set2.topic: Chronic myelogenous leukemia: presentation, diagnosis and phases

set2.q: Which finding favors a reactive leukocytosis over chronic myelogenous leukemia?
opts: Correct. A reactive leukocytosis from infection has no splenomegaly, a white count usually below 50,000, and a negative BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) result. Chronic myelogenous leukemia counts are often above 100,000.
Positive fusion gene by polymerase chain reaction
A positive BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) result is definitive for chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: a reactive count is negative for the fusion gene.
Platelet count above normal with anemia
Elevated platelets with anemia fit the chronic myelogenous leukemia pattern of leukocytosis, thrombocytosis and anemia. Tell: the reactive picture is a modest count without a big spleen.
Abdominal discomfort from a large spleen
Splenomegaly causing abdominal swelling is a feature of chronic myelogenous leukemia; the reactive picture lacks it. Tell: no splenomegaly favors a reactive count.

set2.topic: Acute myeloid leukemia: who and why
set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for disorders of hematological malignancies in the lecture topic list for the following populations. Infant a. child b. adolescent c. adult d. elderly
set2.q: In which group is acute myeloid leukemia mostly seen?
opts: Adolescents are not the group singled out; acute myeloid leukemia is unusual in children outside of neonates. Tell: the named age is adults over 60.
Adults aged 45 to 55 are younger than the group named; acute myeloid leukemia is mostly seen in older adults over 60. Tell: acute myeloid leukemia skews older, over 60.

Correct. Acute myeloid leukemia is mostly seen in adults, particularly older adults over 60, and age over 60 is listed among its risk factors. Its incidence in children is unusual outside of neonates.

Young children are not the group; acute myeloid leukemia is mostly seen in adults, particularly those over 60. Tell: acute myeloid leukemia is unusual in children outside neonates and is an older-adult disease.

set2.q: Which test separates acute lymphoblastic leukemia from the atypical lymphocytosis of mononucleosis or pertussis?
opts: Lumbar puncture checks for central nervous system involvement, an adverse risk factor, after the diagnosis is made. Tell: it stages the leukemia; it does not show whether lymphocytes are clonal.
A chest X-ray may show a mediastinal mass in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, but it cannot tell reactive from malignant lymphocytes. Tell: clonality is read by flow cytometry.
Coagulation tests are part of the wider acute leukemia work-up and matter for bleeding complications. Tell: separating a clone from a reactive infection needs flow cytometry.

Correct. Some infections, including mononucleosis and pertussis, cause atypical lymphocytosis, and flow cytometry differentiates these from acute lymphoblastic leukemia based on its clonal nature. It also shows whether the leukemia is B-cell or T-cell.

set2.topic: Chronic myelogenous leukemia: management and prognosis
set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. set2.q: At 3 months of treatment for chronic myelogenous leukemia, the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level is 25%. Which milestone category is this?
opts: Failure is not defined at 3 months, so even a high level is read as warning at this point. Failure means the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level is above the worst cutoff for that month: above 10% at 6 months, above 1% at 12 months and beyond; it is not defined at 3 months.
Correct. At 3 months, failure is not applicable; the table reads warning above 10% and optimal below 10%. A level of 25% is above 10%, so it is a warning, not yet a failure.
At 3 months, optimal needs a level below 10%, and 25% is above it. Optimal is below 10% at 3 months, below 1% at 6 months, and below 0.1% at 12 months and beyond.

Treatment-free remission is not applicable at 3 months. Treatment-free remission is defined only beyond 18 months, at a BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) level below 0.01%; at earlier months the column is not applicable.

set2.q: What does the fusion protein of chronic myelogenous leukemia do to the cell?
opts: Correct. The chromosome 9 and 22 translocation joins two genes, the BCR-ABL1 (breakpoint cluster region-Abelson 1) fusion, making a functional fusion enzyme that promotes cell proliferation and reduces apoptosis: the cell cannot turn off and constantly divides.
Arrested differentiation at the promyelocyte is acute promyelocytic leukemia, from the chromosome 15 and 17 fusion. Tell: the chronic myelogenous leukemia protein keeps cells dividing.
Elevated cytokines leading to marrow fibrosis come from Janus kinase pathway mutations in myelofibrosis. Tell: the 9 and 22 fusion protein drives proliferation and blocks apoptosis.
Extra chromosome copies, hyperdiploidy, are the favorable childhood finding in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Tell: chronic myelogenous leukemia makes a fusion enzyme, not extra chromosomes.

set2.q: Above what white count does acute myeloid leukemia need emergent leukapheresis?
opts: Thirty thousand is far below the 100,000 count that triggers emergent leukapheresis. Tell: emergent leukapheresis in the myeloid leukemia starts above 100,000.

A white count usually below 50,000 with no splenomegaly describes a reactive leukocytosis from infection, which is separated from chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: leukapheresis in acute myeloid leukemia is triggered above 100,000.

Correct. In acute myeloid leukemia, white counts are often elevated but may be low; unlike acute lymphoblastic leukemia, counts above 200,000 are rare, and every count above 100,000 needs emergent leukapheresis.
Counts above 200,000 are described as rare in acute myeloid leukemia; waiting for that level would be too late. Tell: every count above 100,000 needs emergent leukapheresis.

set2.q: How often does polycythemia vera transform to leukemia?
opts: Correct. Polycythemia vera has an excellent prognosis, with an estimated survival of 14 years, and rarely results in leukemic transformation, in about 5% of cases.
A quarter overstates it; transformation is rare, about 5%. Tell: transformation is rare (about 5%), not a quarter of cases.
About 50% is the recurrence rate after stopping tyrosine kinase inhibitors in chronic myelogenous leukemia. Tell: polycythemia vera transforms in about 5%.
More than 80% within 5 years is the leukemia risk of very high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome. Tell: polycythemia vera rarely transforms.

set2.q: What is the goal of treatment in lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome?
opts: Allogeneic transplant is the only curative option but is high risk with a limited role, and lower-risk disease rarely justifies it. Tell: the low-risk goal is comfort and function.
Cytarabine plus an anthracycline (7+3) is intensive chemotherapy for fit patients with acute myeloid leukemia. Tell: low-risk myelodysplasia is managed for quality of life.
Major molecular response is the treatment target in chronic myelogenous leukemia on tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Tell: the myelodysplasia goal is quality of life.

Correct. Lower-risk myelodysplastic syndrome has a median survival above 5 years and very low risk of acute myeloid leukemia, but patients often have complications from anemia, bleeding or infections, so the goal of treatment is to improve quality of life.

set2.q: About what share of all lymphomas are non-Hodgkin lymphomas?
opts: About 10% is the share of Hodgkin lymphoma, the type characterized by few Reed-Sternberg cells. Tell: the two shares add to 100, and non-Hodgkin is the large majority.
An even split understates non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which makes up about 90% of lymphomas. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma is the small group at about 10%.
Seventy percent understates it; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is about 90% of lymphomas, leaving about 10% for Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: the split is nine to one.
Correct. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for about 90% of all lymphomas and includes both B-cell and T-cell lymphomas. Hodgkin lymphoma, with its Reed-Sternberg cells, makes up the remaining 10%.
